  • Increased hemoglobin concentration: Increasing hemoglobin (e.g., from 10 to 12 g/dl) improves the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. This typically allows the heart to meet the body's oxygen demands with a lower cardiac output, rather than an increased one.
  • Stimulation of carotid body receptors: These receptors respond primarily to low oxygen (Pao2) or high PaCo2. While stimulation can increase heart rate, it is an acute reflex response and does not explain a sustained, significantly higher baseline cardiac output compared to previous catheterization.
  • Transcutaneous nitroglycerin: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator that primarily reduces preload and afterload. While it can improve stroke volume in a failing heart by reducing the workload, its primary effect is not to increase the total cardiac output above healthy or previous baseline levels in this clinical context.

Question: During cardiopulmonary bypass, the perfusionist notes that the mixed venous oxygen saturation has decreased from 65% to 55%. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
description:
During cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), a decrease in mixed venous oxygen saturation indicates that oxygen consumption has increased or oxygen delivery has decreased.

Inadequate muscle relaxation leading to shivering or movement, or increased oxygen demand, is a common cause for a drop in mixed venous oxygen saturation.

Nitroprusside typically improves venous return or reduces resistance but doesn't usually cause a precipitous drop in SvO2 in this context.

Thiopental decreases metabolic rate, which would increase mixed venous oxygen saturation.

Hypothermia (34°C to 28°C) decreases oxygen consumption, thus increasing mixed venous oxygen saturation.

Question: Which of the following pre-existing conditions predisposes to new-onset third-degree heart block during pulmonary artery catheterization?
description:
During pulmonary artery catheterization (insertion of a Swan-Ganz catheter), the catheter must pass through the right ventricle. As it traverses the right ventricular outflow tract, the catheter tip can cause mechanical irritation or trauma to the right bundle branch, leading to a transient right bundle branch block (RBBB) .

In a patient with a pre-existing left bundle branch block (LBBB) , the development of a catheter-induced RBBB results in the complete cessation of electrical conduction between the atria and the ventricles.

This effectively produces a new-onset third-degree (complete) heart block, which can lead to sudden hemodynamic collapse or asystole.

Therefore, patients with known LBBB are considered high-risk during this procedure, and many clinicians recommend having external or transvenous pacing immediately available.

Question: Each of the following statements concerning the activated clotting time (ACT) is true EXCEPT:

options.name: The ACT is prolonged if the specimen is not warmed during the assay
The ACT should be greater than 300 sec before initiating cardiopulmonary bypass
Hypofibrinogenemia may prolong the ACT after cardiopulmonary bypass
Whole blood is used for measurement of the ACT

description:
• EXCEPT (False): The standard ACT target before initiating cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is generally much higher than 300 seconds, typically >400-480 seconds. An ACT of >300 seconds is often used as a minimum, but it is not the standard target to initiate bypass.
  • True: The ACT is commonly used to monitor heparin during CPB because it is more sensitive and linear than the activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) at high blood heparin concentrations (e.g., >2-3 U/mL).
  • True: The ACT is prolonged if the specimen is not warmed during the assay because coagulation is temperature-dependent and slow at lower temperatures.
  • True: Hypofibrinogenemia (low fibrinogen levels) causes, in part, a prolonged ACT.

Question: A 65-kg, 57-year-old man has an initial activated clotting time (ACT) of 122 seconds prior to elective cardiopulmonary bypass. Five minutes after administration of heparin 200 mg, ACT increases to 154 seconds. After two additional doses of 200 mg each from different lots, ACT increases to 240 seconds. The most appropriate next step is to
description:
The scenario describes heparin resistance, defined as the inability to achieve an adequate activated clotting time (ACT) (typically >400–480 seconds for cardiopulmonary bypass) despite the administration of a standard dose of unfractionated heparin (often ~300–400 U/kg).

  • Initial Assessment: The patient received 600 mg total heparin (200 mg x 3) for a 65-kg man, which is a very high dose (>9 mg/kg, equivalent to >900 U/kg, well over the standard 300–400 U/kg), yet the ACT is only 240 seconds, indicating heparin resistance.
  • Most Common Causes: The most frequent cause of heparin resistance is antithrombin (AT) III deficiency.
  • Management: When heparin resistance is suspected (e.g., ACT remains <400–480s despite high-dose heparin), the best next step to avoid further useless heparin administration is to replace AT-III. This is commonly done by administering fresh frozen plasma (FFP) (2 units) or, if available, AT-III concentrate.

Question: Which of the following effects of catecholamine results in the greatest increase in preload?
description:
• Decreased venous capacitance: Catecholamines cause venoconstriction, which reduces the volume of blood that can pool in the venous system (capacitance vessels). This shifts blood from the periphery toward the central circulation, directly increasing preload (the volume of blood returning to the heart).
  • Augmented contractility: This refers to inotropy, which increases the force of contraction but is a consequence of sympathetic stimulation rather than a primary driver of increased preload.
  • Decreased afterload: Decreasing afterload (the resistance the heart pumps against) generally improves stroke volume but does not inherently increase the filling volume (preload).
  • Improved chronotropism: This refers to an increased heart rate. While it increases cardiac output, a very high heart rate can actually decrease preload by reducing the time available for the ventricles to fill during diastole.

Question: Following blunt trauma to the chest, a patient has tachycardia, hypotension, and markedly distended neck veins. Each of the following is expected EXCEPT
description:
• The clinical presentation of blunt chest trauma with tachycardia, hypotension, and distended neck veins (Beck's triad) strongly suggests cardiac tamponade. In this condition, the accumulation of fluid or blood in the pericardial sac compresses the heart, leading to:
  • Decreased Cardiac Output: Pressure on the ventricles limits filling, significantly reducing output (e.g., to 2.1 L/min).
  • Equalization of Pressures: A hallmark of tamponade is that the diastolic pressures in all four heart chambers equalize. This typically manifests as elevated and equal Right Atrial Pressure (RAP), Pulmonary Artery Diastolic Pressure (PADP), and Pulmonary Artery Occlusion Pressure (PAOP/PCWP), often around 25 mmHg.
  • Low Mixed Venous Oxygen Saturation: Because cardiac output is severely low, the tissues must extract more oxygen from the available blood, which typically causes Mixed Venous Oxygen Saturation to drop well below the normal range (normal is ~65–75%). A value of 75% is normal and would not be expected in a state of low-output cardiogenic shock like tamponade.

Question: Which of the following is most likely to result in oxygen desaturation in a patient with Eisenmenger's syndrome who is scheduled for cesarean delivery?
description:
In a patient with Eisenmenger's syndrome, the primary goal of anesthetic management is to maintain the balance between systemic vascular resistance and pulmonary vascular resistance.

Epidural administration of local anesthetics like lidocaine causes a sympathetic blockade, which leads to peripheral vasodilation and a significant decrease in SVR. In Eisenmenger's syndrome, where there is a fixed high PVR and a right-to-left (or bidirectional) shunt, a drop in SVR increases the pressure gradient favoring the right-to-left shunt. This allows more deoxygenated blood to bypass the lungs and enter the systemic circulation, leading to rapid oxygen desaturation and cyanosis.

  • Breathing room air: While supplemental oxygen is preferred to keep PVR low, breathing room air alone is less likely to cause a sudden, catastrophic desaturation compared to a rapid drop in SVR.
  • Intravenous administration of ketamine: Ketamine is often used in these patients because it tends to maintain or slightly increase SVR and does not significantly increase PVR, thus helping to preserve the shunt balance.
  • Intravenous administration of ephedrine: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic that increases SVR (and heart rate), which would generally oppose the right-to-left shunt, making it less likely to cause desaturation than a vasodilator.

Question: A 66-year-old man with aortic regurgitation is brought to the operating room for aortic valve replacement after having received morphine, scopolamine premedication. PO2 is 40 mmHg in a sample of pulmonary artery blood drawn 10 minutes after the patient started breathing pure oxygen. This finding is compatible with
According to the Frank-Starling law, an increase in stroke volume is directly proportional to an increase in which of the following?
description:
The Frank-Starling law states that stroke volume increases in direct proportion to end-diastolic volume (preload) , as greater ventricular filling stretches myocardial fibers, enhancing contraction force.

End-systolic volume reflects afterload effects and decreases with stronger contractions, not causing the increase.

Afterload inversely affects stroke volume.

Heart rate influences cardiac output separately.

Question: Which of the following anesthetic scenarios would cause a patient's Frank-Starling curve to shift downward and to the right?
description:
A downward and rightward shift in the Frank-Starling curve indicates reduced myocardial contractility, where stroke volume decreases for any given preload.

Volatile anesthetics like isoflurane and halothane cause myocardial depression by impairing calcium handling and excitation-contraction coupling, leading to this shift.

Dobutamine and sympathetic activation increase contractility, shifting the curve upward.

Moderate fluid resuscitation moves along the existing curve by increasing preload, without shifting it.

Question: A patient is considered "fluid responsive" if they are operating on which portion of the Frank-Starling curve?

options.name: Fluid responsiveness is independent of the curve position

description: A patient is "fluid responsive" when an increase in preload (e.g., giving a fluid bolus) produces a significant rise in stroke volume or cardiac output, which occurs when the ventricle is on the steep ascending part of the Frank-Starling curve.

Question: Which of the following parameters can be substituted for "Preload" on the x-axis of a Frank-Starling graph in a clinical setting?
description:
The Frank-Starling curve plots cardiac output (or stroke volume) on the y-axis against preload on the x-axis. Preload reflects the degree of myocardial fiber stretch before contraction, mainly driven by end-diastolic volume.

  • In clinical practice, we can't directly measure ventricular end-diastolic volume easily, so we use surrogate markers:

CVP estimates right ventricular preload (via right atrial pressure).

PCWP (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) estimates left ventricular preload (via left atrial pressure).

These pressures correlate with preload in monitoring scenarios like ICU or anesthesia.

  • MAP: Reflects afterload and cardiac output, not preload.
  • SVR: Pure afterload measure (resistance to flow).
  • Cardiac Index: Output metric (y-axis territory), not preload.

Question: A 65-year-old patient under general anesthesia with isoflurane becomes hypotensive, and pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP) is high, but cardiac output (CO) is low. Which of the following best describes the patient's position on the Frank-Starling curve?
description: The patient has high PAOP (high preload) but low CO, i.e., further increases in preload are not increasing stroke volume. That corresponds to the flat (plateau) portion of the Frank-Starling curve.

Question: Following induction of spinal anesthesia, a patient develops severe hypotension. The patient is considered "fluid responsive." Which of the following changes is expected on the Starling curve?

options.name: The curve shifts downward and to the right.
The patient moves down the ascending limb of the curve.
The patient moves up the ascending limb of the curve.
The curve shifts upward and to the left.

description: Spinal anesthesia causes vasodilation and venous pooling, so preload (ventricular end-diastolic volume) falls. Contractility is unchanged, so the Starling curve itself does not shift; instead, the operating point moves down along the same ascending limb (lower preload → lower stroke volume/cardiac output). A "fluid responsive" patient is by definition on the steep/ascending portion, so giving fluid will move them back up that same limb.

Question: A patient in the ICU with a known ejection fraction (EF) of 30% is being managed for septic shock. The Frank-Starling curve for this patient is best described as:

options.name: Shifted downward and to the right (lower slope).

description:
In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF , like this patient's EF of 30%), the Frank-Starling curve flattens and shifts down and right. This reflects poor myocardial contractility—the heart can't generate much stroke volume even with high preload (end-diastolic volume).

  • Normal heart: Steep upward curve; stroke volume rises sharply with preload.
  • Failing heart: Reduced inotropy flattens the slope, max stroke volume is lower, and it needs higher filling pressures (right shift) to achieve any output.

Question: During laparoscopic surgery, the patient is placed in a steep Trendelenburg position. How does this affect the Frank-Starling mechanism?

options.name: Increases venous return, moving the patient up the ascending limb.
Decreases venous return, moving the patient down the ascending limb.

description:
In steep Trendelenburg (head down, feet up), abdominal contents push against the diaphragm, compressing the inferior vena cava and reducing venous return to the right heart. This drops preload.

On the Frank-Starling curve, lower preload shifts the operating point leftward (down the ascending limb) , decreasing stroke volume despite normal contractility.

Question: A 68-year-old male with a history of a massive myocardial infarction one month ago presents with worsening shortness of breath and pedal edema. Echocardiography reveals a reduced ejection fraction of 25%. Which statement best describes the shift in his Frank-Starling curve compared to a healthy individual?

options.name: The curve shifts downward and to the right.
The curve shifts upward and to the left.
The curve remains the same, but the operating point moves left.

description:
Myocardial infarction causes loss of functioning myocardium (negative inotropy). For any given end-diastolic volume (EDV), the stroke volume (SV) is lower, shifting the curve downward. To maintain a near-normal SV, the heart compensates by increasing EDV (moving right along the new curve).

  • The curve shifts upward and to the left: This shift occurs with positive inotropic agents or sympathetic stimulation.
  • The curve remains the same, but the operating point moves left: Moving left on the same curve indicates a decrease in preload (e.g., hemorrhage), which would further decrease CO.
  • The curve becomes steeper: A steeper curve implies increased fluid responsiveness, whereas failing hearts often operate on the "flat" portion of the curve.

Question: A 45-year-old female in the ICU is being treated for septic shock. Her current Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) is 58 mmHg. The clinical team performs a Passive Leg Raise (PLR) test, which results in a 15% increase in her stroke volume. Based on the Frank-Starling mechanism, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.name: No intervention; the patient has reached the "peak" of the curve.

description:
An increase in SV >10-15% after a preload challenge (like PLR or a fluid bolus) indicates the patient is on the ascending (steep) portion of the Frank-Starling curve. This patient is "fluid responsive," meaning more fluid will likely improve cardiac output.

  • Start a vasopressor immediately: While vasopressors may eventually be needed, the positive PLR test specifically confirms that the heart can still increase output with more preload.
  • Administer a diuretic: Diuretics decrease preload. Since she is fluid responsive and hypotensive, decreasing preload would likely cause a further drop in cardiac output.
  • No intervention; the patient has reached the "peak" of the curve: The "peak" or flat portion is reached when SV increases by <10% in response to fluid.

Question: A 65-year-old patient with congestive heart failure is induced with propofol, causing a drop in blood pressure and reduced cardiac output. Which of the following changes would be expected on the left ventricular PV loop?

options.name: Reduced slope of the End-Systolic Pressure-Volume Relationship (ESPVR)

description:
End-systolic pressure–volume relationship (ESPVR) is the line joining all end-systolic points of multiple left-ventricular pressure–volume (PV) loops obtained under different loading conditions.

  • ESPVR slope decreases: Reflects reduced myocardial contractility (inotropy) from propofol. The end-systolic line becomes less steep, shifting downward/leftward.
  • Loop shifts leftward overall (not rightward): Smaller end-diastolic volume from preload reduction (venodilation); reduced stroke volume (not increased).

Isovolumic relaxation time typically shortens with propofol (not increases); it prolongs in hypertrophy or ischemia.

ESPVR slope is the most direct marker of contractility here—blunted in depression, unlike afterload changes (which shift loops rightward without slope change).

Question: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the patient is placed in a steep reverse Trendelenburg position, and pneumoperitoneum is created. How will this affect the PV loop?

options.name: Leftward shift due to decreased venous return (lower preload)

description:
In laparoscopic cholecystectomy with steep reverse Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum, venous return decreases primarily due to the head-up position, leading to reduced preload.

  • PV Loop Effect: This reduced preload causes a leftward shift in the pressure-volume (PV) loop, with decreased end-diastolic volume (EDV) and typically reduced stroke volume.

Question: A patient in the operating room receives a bolus of phenylephrine to treat hypotension. Which of the following best describes the resulting change in the PV loop?
description:
Phenylephrine bolus increases afterload by causing vasoconstriction, raising systemic vascular resistance and arterial pressure.

  • PV Loop Changes: This shifts the isovolumic contraction and end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) leftward/upward on the PV loop. End-systolic volume (ESV) increases because the ventricle cannot eject as much blood against higher pressure, reducing stroke volume (SV = EDV - ESV).

Peak systolic pressure rises due to elevated afterload.

Question: A patient with severe aortic stenosis is undergoing surgery. What is the characteristic feature of their LV pressure-volume loop?

options.name: Much higher systolic pressure and narrower loop

description:
In severe aortic stenosis, the narrowed aortic valve creates high resistance to left ventricular (LV) ejection. This leads to concentric LV hypertrophy, where the ventricle generates much higher systolic pressure to overcome the obstruction and eject blood.

  • The LV pressure-volume (PV) loop reflects this:
  • Higher peak systolic pressure: LV pressure rises sharply during isovolumic contraction and reaches elevated levels (often >200 mmHg) to open the stenotic valve.
  • Narrower loop width: Stroke volume (end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume) decreases due to impaired ejection, reducing the horizontal width of the loop. End-systolic volume increases as the LV struggles to empty fully.
  • Lower peak systolic pressure: Incorrect—pressure is elevated, not lower.
  • Increased width of the loop: Incorrect—width (stroke volume) decreases.
  • Decreased End-Diastolic Pressure: Incorrect—end-diastolic pressure often rises due to diastolic dysfunction from hypertrophy.

Question: During the maintenance phase of general anesthesia with a volatile agent, the patient develops a mild decrease in blood pressure, followed by a compensatory increase in heart rate. Which of the following agents is MOST likely to cause this reflex tachycardia?
description: Desflurane is well-known for causing reflex tachycardia. Unlike some other volatile agents that blunt the baroreceptor reflex, desflurane (especially when the concentration is increased rapidly) can cause a transient surge in sympathetic activity, leading to an increase in heart rate despite a decrease in blood pressure.

Question: A patient receives a rapid 1-litre bolus of intravenous fluids. You observe an increase in heart rate despite the rise in blood pressure. This phenomenon is known as:
description:
The Bainbridge reflex is a cardioacceleratory response triggered by increased venous return and right atrial distension, such as from a rapid fluid bolus.

  • Mechanism: Stretch receptors in the right atrial wall and junction with the vena cava detect rapid volume expansion. Afferent signals travel via the vagus nerve (CN X) to the medulla's nucleus tractus solitarius. This excites the rostral ventrolateral medulla, increasing sympathetic outflow to the sinoatrial node, which raises heart rate and enhances atrial contractility to optimize cardiac output for the increased preload.
  • Key Features:

Occurs despite rising blood pressure (contrasting baroreceptor reflex bradycardia).

Helps prevent venous pooling and maintains stroke volume during hypervolemia.

  • Cushing reflex: Responds to increased intracranial pressure with hypertension and bradycardia, not tachycardia.
  • Celiac reflex: No such cardiac reflex exists; celiac plexus handles visceral sensations, not heart rate changes post-fluid bolus.

Question: A sudden rise in arterial blood pressure leads to which of the following reflex responses?
description:
A sudden rise in arterial blood pressure triggers the baroreceptor reflex (also called the baroreflex).

Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect the stretch from high pressure and send signals via the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves to the brainstem's nucleus tractus solitarius.

  • This leads to:

Increased parasympathetic (vagus nerve) activity, slowing heart rate (bradycardia).

Decreased sympathetic outflow, reducing contractility and vasoconstriction.

The goal is to rapidly lower blood pressure back to normal.

Question: The Bainbridge reflex is specifically triggered by:

options.name: High oxygen tension in the carotid body

Question: The Cushing reflex, often seen in head trauma, is characterized by:
description:
The Cushing reflex is a physiological nervous system response to acute elevations of ICP, resulting in the Cushing triad of widened pulse pressure (increasing systolic, decreasing diastolic), bradycardia, and irregular respirations.

In the first stage of the Cushing reflex, blood pressure and heart rate rise in response to sympathetic activation to overcome increases in ICP.

In the second stage of the Cushing reflex, hypertension continues to be present, but the patient becomes bradycardic rather than tachycardic.

Question: A patient undergoing a long abdominal surgery under general anesthesia becomes hypothermic (34.5°C) and is being hyperventilated to an EtCO2 of 28 mmHg. What is the most likely effect on their OHDC?

options.name: No change in the curve position P50

description:
The Oxyhaemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC) represents the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen and the oxygen saturation of haemoglobin.

A leftward shift indicates that haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen, meaning it binds more tightly and is less likely to release it to the tissues. This is characterized by a decrease in P50 (the partial pressure of oxygen at which 50% of haemoglobin is saturated).

  • In this clinical scenario, two primary factors are causing a leftward shift:
  • Hypothermia (34.5°C): A decrease in body temperature reduces the kinetic energy of molecules, strengthening the bond between oxygen and haemoglobin.
  • Respiratory Alkalosis (Hyperventilation to EtCO2 of 28 mmHg): Hyperventilation reduces PaCO2 levels (hypocapnia), which increases the blood pH (alkalosis). According to the Bohr Effect, a higher pH (lower H+ concentration) and lower PaCO2 both shift the curve to the left.

Question: Which of the following causes a right shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
description:
• A right shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve indicates a decreased affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, meaning oxygen is released more easily to the tissues. This shift occurs in response to factors associated with high metabolic demand:
  • Increased Carbon Dioxide (CO2): High partial pressures of CO2 (pCO2) lead to the formation of carbaminohemoglobin and decrease the pH, both of which stabilize the "T" (tense) state of hemoglobin, favoring oxygen release. This is known as the Bohr effect.
  • Increased Temperature: Higher temperatures (often from exercise or fever) reduce hemoglobin's binding affinity for oxygen.
  • Increased 2,3-BPG: This metabolite binds to deoxyhemoglobin and promotes the release of oxygen.
  • Decreased pH (Acidosis): A higher concentration of hydrogen ions (low pH) encourages hemoglobin to unload oxygen.

Question: What does a "right shift" in the curve indicate?
Which condition would cause a left shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
description:
• Fetal hemoglobin (HbF): This is correct because HbF has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin (HbA). This higher affinity allows the fetus to extract oxygen from the mother's blood across the placenta.
  • Fever: An increase in temperature causes a right shift in the curve, which helps unload oxygen to metabolically active tissues.
  • High altitude: While acute exposure can cause a temporary left shift due to hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis), the body's primary adaptation to high altitude involves an increase in 2,3-DPG levels, which causes a right shift to facilitate oxygen unloading at tissues.
  • Increased exercise: Exercise leads to increased temperature, higher carbon dioxide levels, and lower pH (acidosis) in the muscles, all of which cause a right shift to provide more oxygen to the working muscles.

Question: At a PAO2 of 40mm of Hg (normal tissue levels), hemoglobin is roughly how saturated?
description: At a partial pressure of oxygen (Pao2) of 40 mmHg, which is the typical level in resting body tissues, hemoglobin is approximately 75% saturated. This relationship is defined by the Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve, a sigmoidal (S-shaped) graph that illustrates how hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen changes based on the surrounding environment.

Question: Which of the following shifts the curve to the right?
description: • Decreased pH (Acidosis): A drop in pH (increased H+ concentration) stabilizes the deoxygenated state of hemoglobin (T-state), reducing its affinity for oxygen and shifting the curve to the right. This is known as the Bohr effect.

Question: Which of the following is responsible for the sigmoid shape?
description:
The sigmoid (S-shaped) shape of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve is primarily due to cooperative binding, also known as homotropic allostery.

Hemoglobin consists of four subunits; when the first oxygen molecule binds to one heme group, it causes a structural change (from the Tense "T" state to the Relaxed "R" state) that increases the affinity of the remaining subunits for oxygen.

This makes it progressively easier for the second, third, and fourth oxygen molecules to bind, resulting in the steep middle section of the curve.

Question: In a patient under anesthesia, respiratory acidosis will cause the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to:
description:
• Bohr Effect: As PaCO2 levels rise and pH falls (acidosis), H+ ions bind to specific amino acid residues on hemoglobin. This stabilizes hemoglobin in its deoxygenated T-state (tense state), which has a lower affinity for oxygen.
  • Physiological Impact: A rightward shift means that for any given partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2), hemoglobin binds less oxygen, making it easier for oxygen to be "unloaded" or released into the tissues where it is needed.

Question: Which of the following best describes the effect of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) on the oxygen dissociation curve?
description:
In patients with COPD, the underlying pathology often leads to a rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve. This shift is primarily driven by respiratory acidosis, a condition where the lungs cannot effectively remove carbon dioxide (PaCO2), leading to its accumulation in the blood.

This excess CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogen ions (H+), lowering the blood pH (acidosis).

Question: In metabolically active tissues, the Bohr effect is beneficial because it:
description:
The Bohr effect is a physiological phenomenon where hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen decreases in response to an increase in carbon dioxide concentration and a decrease in pH (increased acidity).

In metabolically active tissues, high levels of CO2 and hydrogen ions (H+) are produced, which trigger this effect to ensure these tissues receive the oxygen they need for cellular respiration (increases oxygen release/unloading).

Question: Which of the following scenarios would produce a "Double Bohr Effect"?

options.name: Transfer of CO2 from fetal to maternal blood, aiding placental CO2 transfer

description:
• The Double Bohr Effect is a specialized physiological mechanism that occurs in the placenta to maximize oxygen delivery to the fetus. It involves two simultaneous shifts of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve (ODC) in opposite directions:
  • Fetal Side: As carbon dioxide (CO2) diffuses from fetal blood into maternal blood, fetal PCO2 decreases and pH increases. This causes a leftward shift of the fetal ODC, increasing the affinity of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) for oxygen, which helps the fetus "grab" oxygen more effectively.
  • Maternal Side: Simultaneously, as the maternal blood receives this CO2 and acid from the fetus, maternal CO2 increases and pH decreases. This causes a rightward shift of the maternal ODC, decreasing the affinity of maternal hemoglobin (HbA) for oxygen and triggering the "unloading" of oxygen toward the fetus.

Question: Which of the following is true about the Haldane effect, often discussed alongside the Bohr effect?

options.name: It explains how O2 concentrations affect hemoglobin's CO2 affinity
It is the opposite of the Bohr effect

description:
The Haldane effect describes how the oxygenation of blood in the lungs displaces carbon dioxide from hemoglobin, facilitating its exhalation. Conversely, in tissues where oxygen levels are low, hemoglobin has a higher affinity for CO2, aiding its transport away from metabolic sites.

  • It is the opposite of the Bohr effect: While the Haldane and Bohr effects are often described as "opposite" in focus (Bohr focuses on O2 affinity, Haldane on CO2 affinity), they are actually complementary mechanisms of the same gas exchange process.
  • It explains O2 loading in tissues: This describes the Bohr effect.
  • It occurs only in the lungs: The Haldane effect occurs in both the lungs (where high O2 causes CO2 release) and the tissues (where low O2 promotes CO2 binding).

Question: Which of the following describes the maternal side of the Double Bohr effect during placental exchange?

options.name: Fetal blood becomes acidic, causing O2 uptake.
Maternal blood becomes acidic due to fetal CO2, shifting the ODC to the right.
Maternal blood becomes alkaline, increasing O2 affinity.
The maternal ODC shifts left to hold onto more oxygen.

Question: In obstetric anaesthesia, maternal hyperventilation can impair fetal oxygenation by:

options.name: Shifting the maternal ODC to the right.
Shifting the maternal ODC to the left, opposing the Double Bohr effect.

description:
Maternal hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, which shifts the maternal oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (ODC) to the left by increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. This left shift hinders oxygen unloading to the fetus at the placenta.

  • The Double Bohr effect normally aids fetal oxygenation: high placental CO₂ and low pH shift the maternal ODC right (facilitating O₂ release), while low fetal CO₂ shifts fetal ODC left (enhancing uptake). Maternal hyperventilation-induced alkalosis opposes this by countering the maternal right shift, impairing O₂ transfer.

Question: Which factor, in addition to the Double Bohr effect, is primary in ensuring the fetus obtains enough oxygen despite low maternal PO2?
description:
In addition to the Double Bohr effect, the higher affinity of HbF for oxygen is a primary mechanism for ensuring the fetus is well-oxygenated.

This occurs because HbF does not bind as effectively to 2,3-DPG (2,3-diphosphoglycerate) as adult hemoglobin (HbA) does. Since 2,3-DPG normally reduces hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen to facilitate unloading at tissues, its lack of effect on HbF keeps the fetal oxygen-dissociation curve shifted to the left, allowing the fetus to "pull" oxygen from the maternal blood even at lower partial pressures.

Question: During the Double Bohr effect, the curves for maternal and fetal hemoglobin:

options.name: Move in the same direction toward the right.
Both shift toward the left to maximize saturation.

description:
• Higher oxygen affinity of Fetal Hemoglobin (HbF): This is the correct primary factor. HbF has a lower P50 (about 19 mmHg) compared to adult HbA (about 27 mmHg), meaning it achieves 50% saturation at a much lower PaO2, facilitating oxygen transfer across the placenta.
  • High maternal 2,3-DPG levels: While maternal 2,3-DPG levels do increase during pregnancy to help unload oxygen to the fetus, this is a maternal adaptation rather than a primary fetal mechanism like the intrinsic property of HbF.
  • Lower hemoglobin concentration in the fetus: This is incorrect. The fetus actually has a higher hemoglobin concentration (approx. 15-20 g/dL) than the mother (approx. 11-12 g/dL), which increases the total oxygen-carrying capacity of fetal blood.
  • Maternal metabolic acidosis: This is incorrect. Maternal blood in the placenta becomes more acidic due to CO2 diffusion from the fetus (the maternal side of the Double Bohr effect), but metabolic acidosis is a pathological state and not a standard physiological mechanism.

Question: A 70 kg patient with a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, SaO2 of 98%, and cardiac output of 5L/min has an approximate oxygen delivery (DO2) of:
description:
Oxygen delivery is calculated as DO₂ = CO × CaO₂

where CO is cardiac output (5 L/min) and CaO₂ (arterial oxygen content) ≈ (1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + (0.003 × PaO₂), with Hb = 10 g/dL and SaO₂ = 0.98.

The dissolved oxygen term is negligible (~0.3 ml/L assuming PaO₂ ≈ 100 mmHg), so CaO₂ ≈ 1.34 × 10 × 0.98 = 13.1 ml/dL = 131 ml/L.

Thus, DO₂ ≈ 5 × 131 = 655 ml/min (rounded to 650-1000 ml/min in MCQ context); closest match is 1000 ml/min.

Question: What is the typical effect of general anesthesia induction on oxygen consumption (VO2) in a resting adult?

options.name: It has no significant effect on VO2
It increases VO2 only if inhalational agents are used

description: Induction of general anesthesia reduces cerebral and whole-body metabolic rate, leading to a modest fall in resting oxygen consumption; textbooks quote a decrease of about 10–15% of basal VO₂, which corresponds to roughly 50–70 mL/min in an average adult.

Question: Which of the following conditions under anesthesia is most likely to increase the oxygen extraction ratio?
description:
In MH, metabolic rate and VO2 rise sharply because of uncontrolled muscle contraction. If oxygen delivery cannot keep up, tissues extract a much larger fraction of delivered O2, so the oxygen extraction ratio increases.

By contrast, barbiturate coma and hypothermia both lower metabolic rate and VO2, decreasing extraction, while high-flow oxygen increases arterial O2 content and typically reduces the extraction ratio.

Question: Which factor would cause an increase in the oxygen extraction ratio?
description:
• Oxygen extraction ratio (OER) is calculated as: OER = (CaO₂ - CvO₂) / CaO₂

It rises when tissues extract more oxygen from blood, widening the arterio-venous O₂ difference.

Decreased mixed venous oxygen tension (PvO₂) directly lowers CvO₂ (since hemoglobin saturation drops via the oxyhemoglobin curve). This increases the numerator, raising OER. Physiologically, this occurs in low-flow states like shock, where tissues extract more O₂ to meet demand.

  • Increased cardiac output: Boosts O₂ delivery, often reducing OER (tissues extract less per unit blood).
  • Increased hemoglobin concentration: Raises CaO₂ (and CvO₂ proportionally), typically keeping OER stable or lowering it.
  • Decreased tissue metabolic rate: Lowers O₂ demand, decreasing extraction and OER.

Question: When calculating O2 consumption during low-flow anesthesia, which parameter is considered?

options.name: (Inspired O2 fraction - End-tidal O2 fraction) X minute ventilation

description:
• O₂ consumption during low-flow anesthesia is estimated from the difference between inspired and expired oxygen, multiplied by minute ventilation:

O₂ consumption ≈ (FIO₂ - FETO₂) × minute ventilation

Question: Pre-oxygenation is performed before induction primarily to:

options.name: Increase the "apnea tolerance time" by building an oxygen reservoir
Ensure 100% saturation for the duration of the surgery

Question: Which anesthetic agent is most likely to cause profound bradycardia due to unopposed vagal activity, especially in children?
description:
Halothane has a potent vagomimetic effect, stimulating the parasympathetic nervous system.

It depresses the SA node and can lead to a shift in the cardiac pacemaker.

It sensitizes the myocardium to catecholamines, which can lead to various arrhythmias, though bradycardia remains a hallmark of its vagal effects.

  • Pediatric vulnerability: Children have a naturally dominant parasympathetic system and higher vagal tone, making them more susceptible to these effects during induction.

Question: A 55-year-old patient with a history of hypertension experiences severe tachycardia and hypertension during tracheal intubation. Which reflex mechanism is being overwhelmed?
description:
The baroreceptor reflex is a rapid negative feedback loop that maintains blood pressure by adjusting heart rate and vascular resistance. In a healthy physiological state, an acute increase in blood pressure (hypertension) should trigger the baroreceptors to decrease the heart rate (bradycardia) to compensate.

During tracheal intubation, the intense sympathetic stimulation often causes a sharp rise in both blood pressure and heart rate. When a patient experiences severe tachycardia and hypertension simultaneously, it indicates that the compensatory mechanism of the baroreceptor reflex—which should have slowed the heart rate in response to the high pressure—has been overwhelmed or bypassed by the massive sympathetic surge.

  • Bainbridge reflex: This reflex increases heart rate in response to increased venous return or right atrial stretch. While it causes tachycardia, it is not the primary mechanism "overwhelmed" during the hypertensive surge of intubation.
  • Cushing reflex: This is a specific response to increased intracranial pressure (ICP), characterized by the triad of hypertension, irregular breathing, and bradycardia.
  • Hering-Breuer reflex: This is a respiratory reflex that prevents lung over-inflation by inhibiting inspiration when pulmonary stretch receptors are activated.

Question: What is the effect of volatile anesthetics (e.g., sevoflurane) on the ANS?
description:
• Dose-Dependent Depression: Sevoflurane and other volatile agents cause a progressive, linear reduction in sympathetic activity and autonomic reflexes as the concentration increases. For example, higher concentrations (above 1 MAC) have been shown to inhibit norepinephrine release and reduce the sensitivity of blood vessels to sympathetic signals, contributing to the decrease in blood pressure.
  • Reflex Inhibition: These agents blunt the body's compensatory mechanisms, such as the baroreflex (the heart's response to changes in blood pressure). At higher doses, they significantly depress somatosympathetic reflexes, which are the body's autonomic responses to pain.

Question: Which of the following neurotransmitters is released by all preganglionic autonomic nerve fibers?
description: In the autonomic nervous system, acetylcholine (ACh) is the universal neurotransmitter released by all preganglionic fibers, regardless of whether they belong to the sympathetic or parasympathetic division. These fibers are classified as cholinergic because they synthesize and release ACh to transmit signals to postganglionic neurons.

Question: Sympathetic postganglionic fibres innervating sweat glands release which neurotransmitter?
description: Sympathetic postganglionic neurons that supply sweat glands are "cholinergic" because they release acetylcholine. This neurotransmitter binds to muscarinic (M3) receptors on the sweat glands to stimulate secretion for thermoregulation.

Question: A patient with a T4 spinal cord injury is undergoing cystoscopy and develops severe hypertension and bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
description:
Autonomic dysreflexia (also known as autonomic hyperreflexia) is a life-threatening medical emergency that occurs in patients with spinal cord injuries at or above the T6 level.

  • Mechanism: A noxious stimulus below the level of injury (in this case, the distention or irritation of the bladder during cystoscopy) triggers a massive, uninhibited sympathetic reflex.
  • Hypertension: The sympathetic surge causes widespread vasoconstriction below the injury level, leading to sudden and severe hypertension.
  • Bradycardia: In response to the high blood pressure, the brain attempts to compensate by sending parasympathetic signals via the vagus nerve to slow the heart, resulting in bradycardia. However, the descending inhibitory signals cannot pass the spinal cord lesion to stop the sympathetic activity below, so the hypertension persists.

Question: Which of the following intravenous anesthetics is known to have significant antimuscarinic (parasympatholytic) properties?
description:
• Antimuscarinic Effects: While ketamine primarily acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, it also exhibits secondary antimuscarinic properties. These properties contribute to its ability to cause bronchodilation, making it a preferred choice for patients with asthma or reactive airway disease.
  • Sympathomimetic Stimulation: Unlike most other intravenous anesthetics, ketamine increases heart rate and blood pressure by stimulating the sympathetic nervous system and inhibiting the reuptake of catecholamines.

Question: During general anesthesia, sudden bradycardia is often due to which of the following?
description:
• Vagal reflex (e.g., traction on peritoneum): Sudden bradycardia during general anesthesia is most commonly caused by the stimulation of the vagus nerve. Common surgical triggers include traction on the peritoneum, pulling on the extraocular muscles (oculocardiac reflex), or carotid sinus stimulation.
  • Increased surgical stimulation: Typically causes tachycardia (increased heart rate) and hypertension as the body responds to pain or stress, especially if the plane of anesthesia is too light.
  • Light anesthesia: Similar to increased surgical stimulation, light anesthesia is associated with tachycardia and hypertension due to an active sympathetic nervous system response.
  • Hypocapnia: Decreased carbon dioxide levels usually lead to a mild increase in heart rate or have minimal effect on it, rather than causing sudden, significant bradycardia.

Question: Using transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), the midesophageal short axis view at 45 degrees shows a valve shaped like the "Mercedes Benz" sign. Which valve is examined in this view?
description:
In transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), the midesophageal short axis view (typically obtained at an electronic rotation of approximately 30 to 60 degrees) is the classic view used to visualize the aortic valve.

  • "Mercedes Benz" Sign: This refers to the characteristic appearance of the three cusps (right coronary, left coronary, and non-coronary) of a normal trileaflet aortic valve when they meet in the center during diastole.

Question: A 47-year-old patient with known hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is anesthetized with propofol and nasally intubated. After induction, his blood pressure rises to 180/120 mm Hg and heart rate rises to 110. One millimeter ST depression is noted on leads I, II, and AVF. Which of the following interventions would be most appropriate at this time?
description:
Esmolol is the most appropriate intervention because it addresses both tachycardia and increased myocardial contractility, which are two of the most critical factors that exacerbate LVOT obstruction in HOCM.

  • Hemodynamic Stability: By slowing the heart rate, Esmolol increases diastolic filling time and maintains left ventricular end-diastolic volume, thereby reducing the outflow gradient.
  • Ischemia Management: Reducing the heart rate and contractility also lowers myocardial oxygen demand, directly treating the ST segment changes.
  • Vasodilators (Nitroprusside/Nitroglycerin): Starting infusions of sodium nitroprusside or nitroglycerin is contraindicated in HOCM. These agents decrease afterload and/or preload, which can significantly worsen the LVOT obstruction and cause a catastrophic drop in cardiac output. Nitroglycerin, in particular, can cause reflex tachycardia, further worsening the obstruction.
  • Desflurane: Deepening anesthesia with a volatile anesthetic like desflurane is inappropriate because desflurane (especially at higher concentrations or during rapid titration) can cause sympathetic activation and tachycardia. Furthermore, volatile agents are vasodilators that reduce systemic vascular resistance (afterload), which is detrimental in HOCM.

Question: A 22-year-old man with HOCM is undergoing an elective cholecystectomy under general anesthesia. Immediately after induction with propofol, 2.5 mg/kg IV, the arterial blood pressure decreases from 140/82 to 70/40 mm Hg. What would be the most appropriate drug for treatment of hypotension in this patient?
description:
In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), the hypotension after propofol induction stems from reduced preload and afterload, which worsens left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. This dynamic obstruction increases further when systemic vascular resistance (SVR) drops.

Phenylephrine, a pure α1-agonist, is ideal because it rapidly increases SVR and blood pressure without boosting heart rate or contractility. This helps maintain afterload to minimize the gradient across the LVOT.

  • Ephedrine: Indirect sympathomimetic that raises HR and contractility via norepinephrine release—increases LVOT obstruction.
  • Epinephrine: Potent β-agonist effects (HR, contractility) worsen obstruction despite α-effects.
  • Isoproterenol: Pure β-agonist; drops SVR further and boosts contractility—strongly contraindicated.

Question: The dose of adenosine necessary to convert paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) to normal sinus rhythm should be initially reduced

options.name: In patients receiving theophylline for chronic asthma
In patients with a history of arterial thrombotic disease taking dipyridamole
In patients with a history of chronic renal failure

description:
Dipyridamole is a drug that inhibits the cellular uptake of adenosine.

  • Potentiation: Because it prevents adenosine from being taken up and broken down by cells, it significantly increases the blood levels and duration of action of adenosine, effectively potentiating its effects.
  • Dose Adjustment: To avoid prolonged bradycardia or other severe side effects, the initial dose of adenosine should be reduced in patients taking dipyridamole.
  • Patients receiving theophylline: Theophylline and other methylxanthines (like caffeine) are adenosine receptor antagonists. They compete for the same receptors, meaning larger doses of adenosine are often required to achieve a therapeutic effect, rather than reduced doses.
  • Patients with chronic renal failure: Renal failure does not significantly alter the rapid metabolism of adenosine. Adenosine is primarily cleared by rapid uptake into erythrocytes and vascular endothelial cells, followed by metabolism to inosine, rather than through renal excretion.
  • Chronic alcoholics: Chronic alcoholism does not have a well-documented clinical requirement for reducing the initial dose of adenosine for PSVT conversion.

Question: PVR as a function of lung volume is the LEAST at which volume?
description:
• At Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) , the total resistance is minimized because it represents the balance point between two types of pulmonary vessels:
  • Alveolar Vessels: These are squeezed as the lungs expand, increasing resistance at high volumes (TLC).
  • Extra-alveolar Vessels: These are pulled open by radial traction as the lungs expand; however, at low volumes (RV), they narrow or collapse, increasing resistance.
  • Equilibrium: FRC is the volume where the combined resistance of these two vessel groups is at its absolute minimum.

Question: A 59-year-old patient is scheduled for right knee replacement. The patient has a long history of CHF with 87% oxygen saturation while breathing room air in the holding area. Rales are audible throughout both lung fields with the patient upright. The MOST appropriate plan would be

options.name: Arterial line and spinal with isobaric bupivacaine
Arterial line, etomidate induction, sevoflurane, intraoperative TEE
Arterial line, CVP line, ketamine induction, N2O narcotic anesthetic, furosemide, milrinone

Question: A 79-year-old patient returns to the operating room with cardiac tamponade after three-vessel coronary artery grafting. In addition to gentle positive pressure ventilation, which of the following permutations in hemodynamics would be MOST beneficial in this scenario?

options.name: Increased preload, slow heart rate, increased afterload
Normal preload, slow heart rate, decreased afterload
Normal preload, fast heart rate, decreased afterload
Increased preload, fast heart rate, increased afterload

description:
• Increased Preload (Volume Expansion): To overcome the high intrapericardial pressure and maximize ventricular filling (Frank-Starling mechanism).
  • Fast Heart Rate (Tachycardia): Tamponade leads to a fixed stroke volume. Therefore, maintaining or increasing the heart rate (tachycardia) is necessary to keep cardiac output (HR × SV) from collapsing.
  • Increased Afterload (Increased Systemic Vascular Resistance): Elevated afterload helps maintain systemic blood pressure in the face of reduced cardiac output, ensuring adequate coronary perfusion pressure, which is vital in a patient who just underwent three-vessel grafting.

Question: Which of the following is responsible for the plateau phase of cardiac action potential?

options.name: Slow movement of potassium out of the cell
Slow movement of calcium into the cell
Slow movement of calcium out of the cell

description:
The plateau phase (Phase 2) of the cardiac action potential is a unique feature of cardiac contractile cells (atrial and ventricular myocytes). It is primarily caused by a sustained influx of calcium ions through voltage-gated L-type (slow) calcium channels.

  • Phase 0: Threshold reached at -70 mV; fast Na+ channels open for rapid upstroke to +30 mV.
  • Phase 1: Early repolarization from Na+ inactivation and transient K+ efflux.
  • Phase 2: Plateau phase (200 ms) due to L-type Ca2+ influx, enabling excitation-contraction coupling.
  • Phase 3: Repolarization as Ca2+ channels close and delayed rectifier K+ channels dominate.
  • Phase 4: Resting potential maintained by Na+/K+ ATPase.

Question: A 2-year-old boy is induced with halothane-inhalation induction. The patient suddenly gets bradycardic, and you decide to administer atropine 0.4 mg intravenously. Immediately thereafter, you notice that the patient is having a junctional tachycardia. Which of the following most accurately describes the sequence of events?

options.name: Sinoatrial (SA) node suppression by halothane followed by anticholinergic action of atropine
Atrioventricular (AV) node suppression by halothane followed by anticholinergic action of atropine
SA node and AV node suppression by halothane followed by anticholinergic action of atropine
SA node and AV node suppression by halothane followed by paroxysmal tachycardic action of atropine

description:
• Mechanism of Bradycardia: Halothane is known to depress the automaticity of the Sinoatrial (SA) node and increase the refractoriness of the Atrioventricular (AV) node. In pediatric patients, this cardiac depression often manifests as significant bradycardia during induction.
  • Response to Atropine: Atropine is an anticholinergic agent administered to reverse bradycardia by blocking vagal tone and stimulating the conduction system.
  • Junctional Tachycardia: Because the SA and AV nodes are still suppressed by the residual effects of halothane, the "higher" pacemakers are inhibited. When the conduction system is stimulated by atropine, the next available tissue in the pathway—the junctional pacemakers—takes over the heart rate, resulting in a junctional rhythm or tachycardia.

Question: Significant intravenous absorption/inadvertent intravenous injection of bupivacaine can cause profound bradycardia and sinus node arrest. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of cardiac toxicity of bupivacaine?

options.name: Bupivacaine binds inactivated fast sodium channels and dissociates from them slowly
Bupivacaine binds activated fast sodium channels and dissociates from them slowly
Bupivacaine binds inactivated slow sodium channels and dissociates from them slowly
Bupivacaine binds activated slow sodium channels and dissociates from them slowly

description:
Bupivacaine, a local anesthetic, causes cardiac toxicity primarily through potent blockade of voltage-gated fast sodium channels (NaV1.5) in cardiac myocytes. It exhibits high affinity for the inactivated state of these channels, binding rapidly during the action potential plateau (fast-in) but dissociating slowly during diastole (slow-out), leading to use-dependent accumulation of block at heart rates of 60-150 bpm.

This slow recovery prolongs the refractory period, slows conduction, reduces excitability, and contributes to bradycardia, arrhythmias, and arrest, explaining bupivacaine's greater cardiotoxicity compared to agents like lidocaine.

Question: The mechanisms of depression of cardiac contractility by volatile anesthetics include all the following, except

options.name: They decrease the entry of calcium into cells during depolarization
They decrease the sensitivity of contractile proteins to calcium

Question: The mechanism of "x" descent (descent between C and V waves) in the right atrial tracing is:

options.name: Downward movement of the atrioventricular (AV) valve cusps after ventricular contraction
Pulling down of the atrium by ventricular contraction
Decline in atrial pressure as the AV valves open

description:
The "x" descent in a right atrial (or jugular venous) pressure tracing is a downward wave that occurs during ventricular systole. It follows the c wave and precedes the v wave.

  • Mechanism: During ventricular contraction, the heart shortens. As the ventricles contract and eject blood, the atrioventricular (AV) ring (the tricuspid valve apparatus in the right heart) is pulled downward toward the apex of the heart. This action increases the volume of the atrium, which leads to a rapid drop in atrial pressure, forming the "x" descent.

Question: A 38-year-old healthy male volunteer is undergoing cardiac function tests as part of a physiology experiment. His vital signs are HR = 62 bpm, BP = 124/74 mm Hg, respiratory rate = 12 breaths/min, SpO2 = 100% on room air, and Hb = 14 g/dL. Which of the following is the best determination of the adequacy of his cardiac output?

options.name: SvO2 of 75% from a pulmonary artery (PA) catheter

description:
This volunteer has normal vital signs, indicating a healthy resting state without signs of distress or compromise.

  • Normal Cardiac Values: Normal cardiac output (CO) at rest is 4-8 L/min (average ~5 L/min). Cardiac index (CI) ranges 2.5-4.0 L/min/m² (upper limit). SvO2 normally 65-75% , reflecting adequate tissue oxygen delivery when normal with normal lactate.
  • SvO2 of 75% (PA catheter): Normal, adequate. Directly reflects balance of oxygen delivery/extraction; normal SvO2 confirms adequate CO without assumptions about BSA or VO2.

Question: Which of the following formulae explains the hypertrophy of heart in response to pressure or volume loads (P, intraventricular pressure; R, ventricular radius; t, wall thickness; T, circumferential stress)?
description:
The relation describing ventricular wall stress and explaining hypertrophy is Laplace's law.

  • For a spherical chamber (like LV): T = (P × R) / (2t)
  • Rearranged to match the options: P = (2Tt) / R

Question: The sinoatrial and the atrioventricular (AV) nodes are supplied in majority of the individuals by
description:
In most individuals, the sinoatrial node and the AV node receive their blood supply from branches of the Right Coronary Artery (RCA) .

  • Right Coronary Artery (RCA): Supplies the right atrium and right ventricle. It typically branches into:
  • Sinoatrial (SA) Nodal Artery: Supplies the heart's natural pacemaker.
  • Posterior Descending Artery (PDA): In most people (70–80%), this comes from the RCA, determining "right dominance". It supplies the bottom of both ventricles and the back of the septum.
  • AV Node Supply: The RCA supplies the AV node in 80–90% of individuals (right-dominant circulation).
  • Left Circumflex Artery (LCx): Supplies the node in approximately 10–15% of cases (left-dominant circulation).

Question: Baroreceptor reflex is ineffective for long-term blood pressure (BP) control because

options.name: Renin angiotensin aldosterone system takes over the control
Renal regulation of BP is more powerful
Of adaptation to changes in BP over 1 to 2 days

description: • Baroreceptor Resetting (Adaptation): If blood pressure remains elevated for a prolonged period (typically 1 to 2 days or more), the baroreceptors "reset" or adapt to this new higher baseline. Once reset, they treat the higher pressure as the new "normal" and stop firing inhibitory signals, thereby losing their ability to bring the pressure back down to a healthy range.

Question: Which of the following portions of myocardium has a dual blood supply?
description:
• According to anatomical studies, the Bundle of His is typically supplied by two different arterial sources: the Atrioventricular (AV) nodal artery (usually a branch of the right coronary artery) and the first septal perforator branch of the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery.
  • Dual Origin: In the vast majority of human hearts, the blood supply to the Bundle of His and its proximal branches is dual in origin.
  • Safety Mechanism: This dual supply provides a protective mechanism; if one of the major coronary arteries is blocked (such as during a myocardial infarction), the conduction system may still receive enough blood from the other source to function, potentially preventing complete heart block.
  • Atrioventricular node: The AV node is primarily supplied by a single source, the AV nodal artery, which arises from the right coronary artery in about 80-90% of people (right-dominant hearts).
  • Posterior papillary muscle: This muscle is generally considered to have a single blood supply from the right coronary artery (or sometimes the circumflex artery), making it more vulnerable to ischemia and rupture during a heart attack.
  • Sinoatrial node: The SA node is typically supplied by a single artery, the Sinoatrial nodal artery, which originates from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of individuals and from the left circumflex artery in the remaining 40%.

Question: Which of the following types of myocardial work needs the highest oxygen requirement?
description:
Pressure work (also called tension work or internal work) is the primary determinant of myocardial oxygen consumption because the heart must generate significant intramyocardial wall tension to overcome afterload and open the semilunar valves.

  • Why Pressure Work is the Correct Choice:
  • High Energy Demand: Pressure work involves the "isovolumetric" phase where the heart develops high tension without changing volume. This process is metabolically inefficient, requiring significantly more oxygen than moving a volume of blood.
  • Clinical Significance: Conditions that increase pressure work, such as hypertension or aortic stenosis, lead to a much steeper rise in oxygen demand compared to conditions that increase volume work, such as exercise-induced increases in stroke volume.
  • Electrical activity: The energy required for the conduction and propagation of electrical impulses (depolarization and repolarization) is negligible, accounting for less than 1% of the heart's total oxygen consumption.
  • Volume work: Also known as external work or "stroke work," this is much more efficient than pressure work. The heart can increase its output by increasing volume (preload) with a relatively small increase in oxygen cost compared to increasing pressure.
  • Basal requirement: While the heart has a high basal metabolic rate to maintain cellular integrity and ionic gradients even at rest, this "maintenance" energy is lower than the active energy required for mechanical pressure generation.

Question: Which of the following inhalational agents causes the least coronary vasodilation?

A 67-year-old patient with uncontrolled hypertension presents for an elective dialysis access creation. Which of the following techniques is not suited for attenuating the hypertensive response to intubation?
description:
• Lidocaine 0.5 mg/kg IV: This dose is generally considered insufficient to attenuate the hypertensive response. Studies suggest that a dose of 1.5 mg/kg administered approximately 3 minutes before intubation is required to effectively suppress the cough reflex and hemodynamic response.
  • Fentanyl 3 μg/kg IV: Opioids like fentanyl are highly effective at blunting the sympathetic response. A dose of 3 μg/kg is a standard and effective choice.
  • Topical airway anesthesia: Applying local anesthetic directly to the airway (e.g., lidocaine spray) reduces the sensory input from the larynx and trachea, thereby decreasing the reflex sympathetic surge.
  • Esmolol 1 mg/kg IV: Esmolol is a short-acting beta-blocker frequently used for this exact indication. A dose of 1 mg/kg given shortly before induction is a well-established technique to control heart rate and blood pressure spikes during intubation.

Question: Which of the following antianginal agents has the highest coronary vasodilating potential?
description:
• Dihydropyridines: These agents are the most potent vasodilators in the group. They specifically target the L-type calcium channels in the smooth muscle of blood vessels, including the coronary arteries, leading to significant vasodilation.
  • Nitrates: While nitrates are classic vasodilators, their primary therapeutic effect in angina is venodilation (widening of the veins), which reduces the "preload" or workload on the heart. Their effect on coronary arteries is significant but typically considered less potent than that of dihydropyridines for direct arterial dilation.
  • Verapamil: This is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. While it does dilate coronary arteries, it is much more "cardiac selective," meaning it has a stronger effect on slowing heart rate and reducing heart muscle contraction than on dilating blood vessels.
  • β-Blockers: These agents are not vasodilators. In fact, they work by blocking the effects of adrenaline, which slows the heart rate and reduces the force of contraction to lower oxygen demand. In some cases, they can even cause slight vasoconstriction as a side effect.

Question: Which of the following statements about calcium channel blockers (CCBs) is not true?

options.name: CCBs potentiate both depolarizing and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers
CCBs potentiate the circulatory effects of volatile anesthetic agents
Verapamil has no effect on cardiac contractility; it acts only on the atrioventricular (AV) node

description:
• Verapamil has no effect on cardiac contractility; it acts only on the atrioventricular (AV) node: This statement is NOT true. Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that has significant negative inotropic effects (decreases cardiac contractility) in addition to its effects on the AV node (negative chronotropy and dromotropy).
  • CCBs potentiate both depolarizing and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers: True. Calcium is essential for the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction and for muscle contraction. By inhibiting calcium entry, CCBs can enhance the effects of muscle relaxants.
  • CCBs potentiate the circulatory effects of volatile anesthetic agents: True. Both CCBs and volatile anesthetics (like halothane or isoflurane) can cause vasodilation and myocardial depression. When used together, they have an additive effect on lowering blood pressure and heart rate.
  • Verapamil may decrease anesthetic requirements: True. Research indicates that calcium channel blockers like verapamil can reduce the Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) of volatile anesthetics, meaning less anesthetic is needed to achieve the same effect.

Question: Which of the following β-blockers is most suited for a patient with bronchospastic disease?
description:
• Metoprolol: This is a cardioselective beta 1-blocker. It primarily targets beta 1 receptors in the heart rather than beta 2 receptors in the lungs. By avoiding beta 2 blockade, it reduces the risk of causing bronchoconstriction, making it a safer choice for patients with asthma or COPD.
  • Bisoprolol: This is also a highly cardioselective beta 1-blocker and is often considered one of the safest options for patients with respiratory disease.
  • Propranolol: This is a non-selective beta-blocker that blocks both beta 1 and beta 2 receptors. Blocking beta 2 receptors in the lungs leads to smooth muscle contraction and bronchoconstriction, which can trigger a severe or fatal asthma attack.
  • Acebutolol: While acebutolol is cardioselective, it also possesses intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA). While it is generally safer than propranolol, it is typically not the "most suited" or first-line recommendation when more established cardioselective agents like metoprolol or bisoprolol are available.

Question: A 24-year-old female patient with a preoperative QTc interval of 550 ms is undergoing breast surgery under general anesthesia. Droperidol is administered to the patient for prevention of postoperative nausea, following which the patient goes into polymorphic-ventricular tachycardia. Which of the following drugs/therapies is best for the patient at this point?
description:
This patient is experiencing Torsades de Pointes (TdP) , a specific type of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) triggered by the administration of droperidol in the presence of a pre-existing long QTc interval.

  • Mechanism: Overdrive transvenous pacing (typically at rates of 90-110) is a highly effective treatment for drug-induced TdP. It works by shortening the QT interval and decreasing temporal dispersion of repolarization, which suppresses the early afterdepolarizations (EADs) that trigger the arrhythmia.
  • Standard Management: While intravenous magnesium sulfate is usually the first-line pharmacologic agent, pacing is the preferred definitive therapy for patients who are refractory to magnesium or as a primary intervention to prevent recurrent pause-dependent TdP.
  • Amiodarone: This is contraindicated in this scenario. Amiodarone itself can prolong the QT interval and would likely worsen the underlying condition.
  • Lidocaine: While occasionally used as a second- or third-line agent for TdP, it is generally considered ineffective or only temporarily beneficial, with TdP frequently recurring.
  • Diltiazem: This is a calcium channel blocker used primarily for supraventricular tachycardias and certain idiopathic VTs. It is not a standard treatment for TdP.

Question: Which of the following factors is not associated with severe multivessel disease during exercise electrocardiography?

options.name: Sustained decrease (≥10 mm Hg) in systolic blood pressure during exercise
Failure to reach a maximum heart rate greater than 70% of predicted
Persistence of ST-segment depression after exercising for 5 minutes or longer

description:
• Normal Variant: During exercise, the J-point often becomes depressed, and the ST segment becomes sharply upward sloping toward the baseline. This pattern, even if it reaches 1 mm, is generally non-ischemic unless it is "slowly upsloping" (defined as reaching > 1.5 mm at 80 ms after the J-point).
  • Sustained decrease (> 10 mm Hg) in systolic blood pressure during exercise: This is a highly specific marker for severe CAD and left ventricular dysfunction.
  • Failure to reach a target heart rate (chronotropic incompetence): This is associated with a higher likelihood of obstructive CAD and a poorer prognosis.
  • Persistence of ST-segment depression for 5 minutes or longer during recovery: This is a strong predictor of severe multivessel disease and adverse outcomes.

Question: Adverse effects of hypothermia include all the following, except
description:
• Irreversible coagulopathy: This is the incorrect statement (the "except"). While hypothermia significantly interferes with the coagulation cascade—specifically by slowing the enzymatic reactions required for clot formation—these effects are physiological and temperature-dependent. The coagulopathy is generally corrected as the body temperature returns to normal.
  • Platelet dysfunction: Hypothermia is well-known to cause reversible platelet dysfunction. Low temperatures impair platelet aggregation and adhesion.
  • Potentiation of citrate toxicity: Hypothermia reduces the metabolic rate of the liver. Since the liver is responsible for metabolizing citrate (an anticoagulant used in blood products), hypothermic patients are at a higher risk of citrate toxicity and subsequent hypocalcemia during massive transfusions.
  • Depression of myocardial contractility: As core temperature drops, there is a direct depressant effect on the myocardium, leading to decreased cardiac output, bradycardia, and a reduction in myocardial contractility.

Question: Coronary perfusion pressure is

options.name: Arterial diastolic pressure - left-ventricular end diastolic pressure
Arterial diastolic pressure - left-ventricular end systolic pressure
Arterial systolic pressure - left-ventricular end diastolic pressure
Arterial systolic pressure - left-ventricular end systolic pressure

description:
Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is the pressure gradient driving blood flow through the coronary arteries to the myocardium, primarily during diastole when the heart relaxes.

The standard formula for CPP is aortic (or arterial) diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) , as this reflects the net driving pressure across the coronary bed.

Question: Which of the following is not an indication of low flow rates under cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)?

options.name: Hypoxemia noticed on an in-line venous oxygen saturation monitor

description:
Low flow rates during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) cause inadequate tissue perfusion, leading to increased oxygen extraction and a drop in mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2).

SvO2 typically falls below 75% in low flow states, so a value >80% indicates adequate flow rather than low flow.

Question: Discontinuing ventilation prematurely before full flow is achieved on cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) causes

options.name: Helps to increase venous return via the venous outflow cannula
Aids the surgeon to visualize and cannulate the coronary sinus

description:
Discontinuing ventilation prematurely before achieving full CPB flow leads to lung collapse or atelectasis, which increases intrapulmonary shunting.

This creates a right-to-left shunt where deoxygenated blood bypasses ventilated alveoli, causing systemic hypoxemia.

Additionally, during partial CPB, factors like a sucking LA vent can cause paradoxical interatrial right-to-left shunting across a patent foramen ovale or atrial septum defect, exacerbating hypoxemia.

  • Increased dead space: This is incorrect because stopping ventilation leads to alveolar collapse (atelectasis) and shunting, rather than just ventilating areas with no blood flow (dead space).
  • Helps to increase venous return: Stopping ventilation actually reduces the intrathoracic pressure swings that normally assist venous return.
  • Aids the surgeon to visualize and cannulate the coronary sinus: Ventilation is typically paused to provide a still surgical field or to deflate the lungs for better access to the heart once full flow is established, but doing so prematurely (before full flow) is a safety risk.

Question: Which of the following is the most sensitive to detect air bubbles at the termination of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)?
description:
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is considered the most sensitive clinically available modality for detecting air bubbles (emboli) during and at the termination of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). It can detect minute amounts of air, as little as 0.02 mL/kg.

  • Doppler ultrasonography: While Doppler (specifically precordial Doppler) is highly sensitive, it is generally less sensitive than TEE.
  • Manual visualization: This method relies on the surgeon seeing bubbles in the heart or bypass circuits. It is the least sensitive.
  • Epiaortic echocardiography: While epiaortic imaging is highly sensitive for detecting atherosclerotic plaques in the ascending aorta, it is not the primary or most sensitive tool specifically for general air bubble detection at the termination of CPB.

Question: Inhaled nitric oxide (NO) at 60 ppm has all of the following effects, except
description:
Inhaled Nitric Oxide (iNO) is a selective pulmonary vasodilator. Because it has an extremely short half-life (seconds) and is rapidly inactivated by binding to hemoglobin when it reaches the bloodstream, it generally does not reach the systemic circulation in significant enough concentrations to cause systemic effects like a drop in SVR.

  • Drop in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR): This is the primary therapeutic effect. iNO relaxes the smooth muscles in the pulmonary blood vessels, directly lowering PVR and mean pulmonary arterial pressure.
  • Improvement in cardiac output: By reducing the afterload on the right ventricle, iNO can improve right ventricular function and subsequently increase overall cardiac output.
  • Better right coronary perfusion: As the pulmonary artery pressure and right ventricular (RV) wall tension decrease, the compression on the right coronary arteries (which supply the RV) is reduced. This leads to improved oxygen delivery and perfusion to the right myocardium.

Question: The central venous pressure (CVP) waveform in cardiac tamponade is characterized by
description:
In cardiac tamponade, the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space increases pressure throughout the cardiac cycle. This compression specifically interferes with the heart's ability to fill during early diastole, which is normally represented by the y descent.

  • Mechanism: The "y" descent in a central venous pressure (CVP) or jugular venous pulse (JVP) waveform represents the rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle following the opening of the tricuspid valve.
  • Tamponade Effect: Because the high intrapericardial pressure resists the expansion of the right ventricle, blood cannot flow quickly from the atrium to the ventricle during early diastole. This leads to a blunted or absent (abolished) y descent.
  • Diagnostic Clue: A prominent y descent actually excludes severe cardiac tamponade and is instead more characteristic of constrictive pericarditis.

Question: In constrictive pericarditis

options.name: Increased diastolic filling does not occur, in contrast to acute tamponade
The Y descent is absent in CVP waveform
Diffuse T-wave abnormalities are a rare sign

description:
• Pulsus paradoxus is uncommon: While pulsus paradoxus (a drop in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration) is a hallmark of cardiac tamponade, it is generally not found in constrictive pericarditis (occurring in only about 20% of cases). This is because, in constriction, the rigid pericardium often prevents the respiratory-related changes in filling that drive the paradox.
  • Increased diastolic filling does not occur: This is incorrect because early diastolic filling in constrictive pericarditis is actually rapid and increased due to high atrial pressures. Filling only stops abruptly when the heart hits the limit of the rigid pericardium (the "knock").
  • The Y descent is absent in CVP waveform: This is incorrect. In constrictive pericarditis, the y descent is sharp and prominent (part of the "W" or "M" shaped waveform) due to the rapid early diastolic filling. An absent or attenuated y descent is actually a characteristic of cardiac tamponade.
  • Diffuse T-wave abnormalities are a rare sign: This is incorrect. ECG changes, including diffuse T-wave flattening or inversions, are actually very common findings in chronic constrictive pericarditis.

Question: Normal mixed venous oxygen tension is ______ (mm Hg):
description:
40 mm Hg is the standard normal value for mixed venous oxygen tension.

  • Mixed Venous Blood: This is a mixture of venous blood returning from all parts of the body (superior and inferior venae cavae). It is ideally sampled from the pulmonary artery using a catheter.
  • Clinical Significance: A drop in MVO2 below 40 mm Hg can indicate that tissues are extracting more oxygen due to decreased oxygen delivery (e.g., low cardiac output or anemia) or increased metabolic demand.
